analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse-to-patient staffing ratios in hospitals to protect patient safety.
analysis.headline: The bill had 57 Democratic cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees until Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every hospital to keep a minimum number of registered nurses on each unit at all times — for example, no more than four patients per nurse on a medical-surgical ward and no more than two in intensive care. Hospitals would have to post the actual ratios each shift, keep records, and submit staffing plans to the Department of Health and Human Services, which could fine hospitals up to $50,000 for repeat violations and publish the names of penalized hospitals. Nurses would gain the right to refuse an assignment that violates the ratios or that they are not trained for, with federal protection against retaliation. Medicare payments to hospitals would be adjusted to cover the extra costs of caring for Medicare patients under the new ratios, and the bill adds stipends to the nurse scholarship program and expands nurse retention grants.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who would get more nursing time at the bedside, and nurses, who would get enforceable workload limits, protection from retaliation for refusing unsafe assignments, and whistleblower protections for patients and staff who report understaffing.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must implement staffing plans with minimum ratios by unit: 1 nurse per patient in trauma and operating rooms, 2 in critical care, 3 in emergency rooms and pediatrics, 4 in medical-surgical units, 5 in rehab, and 6 in postpartum and well-baby units.

Hospitals must post actual nurse-to-patient ratios in each unit each shift and keep three years of records available to the Secretary of Health and Human Services, nurses, their unions, and the public, with periodic federal audits.

A nurse may refuse an assignment that violates the ratios or that she is not competent to perform without risking patient safety, and the hospital may not fire, retaliate, or report her to a state licensing board for it; nurses and patients can win reinstatement, back pay, and attorneys' fees in federal court.
The bill bans averaging ratios across units, bans using mandatory overtime to meet the ratios, and bans substituting video monitors for direct observation by a nurse.
Medicare payments to hospitals would be increased by the net cost of complying with the ratios for Medicare patients, and rural hospitals get up to four years to phase in compliance.
The bill adds stipends to the federal nurse scholarship program and expands nurse retention grants to fund preceptorship and mentorship programs for new nurses.

analysis.who_pays: Hospital operators, who would have to hire many more registered nurses and ancillary staff; the federal Medicare program would cover the portion of those costs attributable to Medicare patients, but hospitals would absorb the costs of staffing for privately insured patients.

drawbacks.text: The ratios are fixed numbers by unit type, which hospitals argue cannot adjust for how sick patients are on a given shift; the bill addresses this partly with acuity-based rules allowing additional staffing above the minimums, but the floor itself is rigid.

Hiring enough nurses to meet the ratios is a large cost; the bill offsets only the costs attributable to Medicare patients through payment adjustments, leaving hospitals to absorb staffing costs for privately insured patients, which could be passed to insurers and patients through hospital charges or premiums.

Rural hospitals, where nurse recruitment is hardest, face a real feasibility problem even with the four-year phase-in; if they cannot recruit the nurses, they could face penalties for shortfalls they cannot fix.
The bill creates emergency and state-of-emergency exemptions, but deciding when those apply would rest on federal guidance and complaint-driven enforcement, which hospitals would contest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-safety benefit is backed by the findings in the bill itself, including studies cited that California's staffing ratios improved patient outcomes and nurse retention and that increased nurse staffing improved quality with no additional cost. The main cost is hospitals' need to hire more nurses, which is partly a real expense and partly a transfer from hospital margins to nurses' paychecks; the Medicare offset covers only the Medicare share of the cost, and rural feasibility is a genuine concern. The bill's strong enforcement, transparency, and anti-retaliation provisions make it more than a paper standard, but its fixed ratios are a blunt tool compared with pure acuity-based staffing.

outcome.mechanism: It died in committee: the House sent it to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to a health subcommittee, and neither took it up before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 4, 2017 by Rep. Janice Schakowsky and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees.
Within two weeks it was referred to the Health Subcommittee in each committee chain, and no markup, hearing, or floor vote followed.
It had 57 cosponsors, all Democrats, by the end of the Congress.
The bill would have been enforced through Medicare and Medicaid participation requirements, so any hospital taking federal health program payments had to comply.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital operators, who avoided a federal mandate to hire more nurses and the exposure of public staffing records and fines. Nurses and patients gained nothing; understaffing remained governed by state rules, with California as the only state with ratios.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospital operators who avoided staffing mandates

against.what_they_did: The hospital industry opposed federal nurse staffing ratio mandates, arguing fixed ratios raise labor costs and reduce staffing flexibility.

sides.party_line_note: All 57 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call test of party or bipartisan support exists.

industries.note: Hospitals would have to hire substantially more registered nurses, post their real staffing ratios publicly, keep auditable records, and face civil fines up to $50,000 per repeat violation. Medicare payment adjustments would cover only the Medicare share of the added cost, so hospitals would bear the rest. Hospital operators' profit depends on keeping staffing lean, which puts their interest against the bill's patient-safety mandate.

industries.industry: Temporary and agency nurse staffing firms
industries.note: Meeting the ratios would require hiring many more nurses, increasing demand for contract nurses; but the bill requires agency nurses to demonstrate unit competence and complete hospital orientation before assignment, which raises the bar for how they can be used.

Nurses would get enforceable workload limits, guaranteed breaks with competent relief, protection from retaliation for refusing unsafe assignments, and a formal role on hospital staffing committees. Better retention and workload is the bill's stated recruitment tool for addressing the nursing shortage.
